title: Payroll Workflow: Start to Finish
subtitle: Corporate Technology Services  ·  Employment Hero Payroll  ·  Fortnightly cycle  ·  Including approver responsibilities and approval emails

blocks.text: About this workflow

This is the whole payroll cycle: the order it runs in, when each stage happens, who is accountable for each check, what must be true before you move on, and what happens when something is not ready in time.

It does not repeat the screen-by-screen instructions. The parts of the Payroll Processing Manual tell you how to do each step and the checklist workbook is what you tick as you go. This document is the map and the rules of engagement: read it first, work from the manual and the checklist on the day.

How to do each step, screen by screen
The steps in order, ticked off as you work the fortnight
The same walkthrough as spoken text, for revision away from the desk
The questions the training recordings never answered

blocks.label: Two kinds of content, marked throughout.
blocks.text: Most of this document describes the process as it was recorded and written up in the manual. The responsibility model in the next section is different: it is a change to how payroll operates, setting out that approving managers carry the timesheet, roster, overtime and time in lieu checks and the liability that goes with them. Anything that is a change rather than a description is marked as such, and the sections it contradicts in the existing manual are listed at the end.
Who is responsible for what

blocks.label: This section is a process change, not a description of current practice.
blocks.text: It needs sign-off from Duncan and Graham before it takes effect, and it contradicts parts of the existing manual until those are updated. See What this changes elsewhere at the end of this document.

Payroll processing and payroll authorisation are two different jobs, and they have been running together. Separating them is standard practice and it is the single biggest control improvement available here: the person who knows what was actually worked approves it, and the person who processes the pay applies what was approved.
The principle, in one line

blocks.label: The approver owns what was worked. Payroll owns that what was approved is paid correctly.
blocks.text: A manager approving a timesheet is certifying that the hours are true, that they were authorised, that any overtime and time in lieu are correct against the roster, and that the cost centre is right. Payroll takes that certification at face value and processes it. Payroll does not re-verify it, does not reconstruct it from the roster, and does not carry the consequences of an approval that turns out to be wrong.
The test: two questions
When a question arises mid pay run, sort it with these two questions. They settle almost everything.

rows: Is it a question about what happened?
The approver's. Did they work it, was it authorised, was it overtime, was it time in lieu, which cost centre. Query it back; do not answer it yourself.
Is it a question about how approved work is paid?
Payroll's. The award rate, the matrix rate, the multiplier, the superannuation treatment, what the system did with it. Answer it and apply it.

blocks.text: The responsibility matrix
Accountable means the person who carries it if it is wrong. Payroll's column says what payroll does with the result, which in most rows is apply it, not check it.

blocks.text: What payroll no longer does
These stop, and stopping them is the point of the change. Each one is a check that payroll cannot perform reliably because payroll was not there when the work happened.
Comparing actual times against the roster to decide whether hours are genuine
Working out whether a long day was authorised overtime or just a long day
Deciding whether hours should have been overtime or time in lieu
Reconstructing someone's fortnight from the shared calendar or the rostering view because the timesheet looks wrong
Chasing an approving manager repeatedly after the cut-off has passed
Estimating, accruing or manually entering hours that were never approved

blocks.label: Payroll does not fix an approver's work.
blocks.text: Where payroll notices something that looks wrong, it goes back to the approver as a query with a deadline, not into the pay run as a correction. A silent fix by payroll takes the liability back off the approver, which defeats the whole arrangement, and it means nobody learns that the approval was wrong.
What payroll still owns, and must keep doing
The change moves verification, not compliance. Payroll remains the control that stops a non-compliant payment going out, and these are not negotiable regardless of what a manager approved.
Applying the Live Performance Award correctly to approved casual hours, including the 38-hour weekly and 8-hour daily overtime thresholds
Applying the CTS Overtime Matrix correctly to approved salaried overtime
Applying the award meal-break consequence where the record shows a break was not taken, including the penalty past five continuous hours
Stopping the system paying the same hours as both daily and weekly overtime, which overpays the employee
Handling the 8-hour rounding rule so a salaried employee is neither over nor under paid by it
Verifying every pay rate, and overriding a rate that failed to sync from HR
Balancing the pay run to zero before it is finalised
Superannuation, PAYG, salary sacrifice, record keeping and the ATO lodgement

blocks.label: An approval does not override the award.
blocks.text: If a manager approves something the award does not permit, payroll does not pay it. Payroll applies the award and raises the conflict with the approver and with Graham. Approver accountability covers what was worked; it does not authorise a non-compliant payment.
The limit of this arrangement
Be clear about what this does and does not achieve, because it is easy to overstate.

Internally, it allocates accountability: an approving manager is answerable for an approval that was wrong, and payroll is answerable for processing an approval incorrectly. That is real, it is enforceable through the business, and it is the right way round.

blocks.label: It does not move the employer's legal obligation.
blocks.text: CTS remains the employer, and the employer carries the statutory obligations: paying correctly under the award and the Fair Work Act, and keeping compliant time and wages records. No internal allocation of duties shifts that to an individual manager. This is an internal accountability model and an audit trail, not a transfer of legal liability away from the business. Have Duncan or Graham confirm the wording before it is circulated, and get it checked by whoever advises CTS on employment matters if it is going into a policy.
The 10am Monday cut-off, and what happens when it is missed

The cut-off only works if there is a consequence attached to it, and the consequence has to be the same every fortnight. Without one the cut-off is a suggestion, payroll absorbs the slippage, and the liability quietly comes back to payroll.
The consequence: missing time is paid in the next pay run

blocks.label: Any time not approved by 10am Monday is paid in the following pay run.
blocks.text: It is not estimated, not manually entered, and not held while someone is chased. It drops out of the current fortnight and is picked up as a back pay in the next one. This applies whether the timesheet was never submitted, was submitted and never approved, or was approved after the cut-off had passed.
Three reasons this is the right answer, and they are worth being able to say out loud when someone pushes back:

It is already the established process for a related case. An expense submitted after the cut-off goes into the following pay run, and has done since 2024. There is no good reason for hours to work differently
The alternative is payroll entering unapproved hours, which is precisely the thing this change exists to stop
Nothing is lost. The employee is paid for every hour they worked; the payment is one fortnight later, with the delay attributable to the approval, not to payroll

rows: Drops out. Paid next fortnight once submitted and approved
Submitted but not approved by 10am Monday
Drops out. Paid next fortnight once approved
Approved in time but wrong, and queried back
Payroll holds it only until the pay run is finalised. If the approver has not responded by then, it drops out and is paid next fortnight
The approved shifts are paid this fortnight. The missing ones drop out
Do not absorb this as a payroll problem. Escalate it and let the escalation decide whether the pay date moves

blocks.label: Say it in advance, every fortnight, in writing.
blocks.text: The consequence is only defensible if the approvers were told before the cut-off, not after. That is what the reminder emails below are for, and it is why they all state the consequence in the same words. Keep the sent emails with the fortnight's records; they are the evidence that the approver was given notice.
The reminder and escalation timetable

Four emails per fortnight, on a fixed schedule. They are templates, not drafting exercises: send them as they are so that the wording is identical every fortnight and nobody can argue they were told something different this time.

rows: E1  Advance notice to all approvers
Gives two working days before the period even closes
E2  Period closed, approvals due Monday 10am
Names who is outstanding while there is still time
E3  Final call, two hours remaining
Last chance, with the consequence stated plainly
Records what dropped out and who it belonged to

blocks.text: The escalation ladder

This ladder is proposed. The training recordings never covered escalation and the handover document lists it as an open question, so it needs Duncan and Graham to agree the steps and the names before the first fortnight it is used.

rows: E4 to the approving manager, copying their department head, Graham and Duncan. Lists exactly which employees and shifts have dropped out
Proceeds with the pay run without the unapproved hours. Does not wait
Resolves it with the approver for next fortnight. Payroll is not involved
Notifies the affected employees that part of their time moves to the next pay run, naming the approval as the reason
Pays the back pay in the normal run. Nothing special is required

blocks.label: Who tells the employee is a decision to make, not a detail.
blocks.text: Step 4 as written has payroll notifying the employee. There is a reasonable argument that it should be the approving manager, since it was their approval that delayed the pay and payroll telling the employee puts payroll in the middle of it. Settle this before the first time it happens rather than during it. The template at E6 is written for payroll sending it; it is easily reworded if the decision goes the other way.
The emails: ready to send
Seven templates. The first four are the fortnightly cycle and go out every fortnight without exception. The last three are situational. Square brackets are the only things you change.

blocks.label: Do not soften them.
blocks.text: The tone is deliberately flat and factual. These emails exist to create a record that notice was given, so they state the deadline, the consequence and who is responsible, and they do not apologise for it. An email that hedges the consequence is an email that cannot be relied on later.
E1  Thursday, advance notice

blocks.subject: Action required: timesheet approvals due 10am Monday [DD Mon] - fortnight ending [DD Mon]
body: Hi all,
The current pay fortnight closes this Friday [DD Mon]. All timesheets for the period [DD Mon] to [DD Mon] must be approved in Employment Hero by 10am Monday [DD Mon].
When you approve a timesheet you are confirming, for each person in your team:
The hours recorded are the hours actually worked
The actual times reconcile to the roster, or the difference is accounted for

Any overtime was authorised in advance by you, and the approval is attached to the timesheet showing the reason, whether it is chargeable to the client, and whether it is being taken as pay or as time in lieu
Any time in lieu accrued or taken is correct against the roster
Meal breaks are recorded accurately, including where a break was not taken
The cost centre on each shift is correct
Payroll processes what has been approved. Payroll does not check hours against the roster and does not decide whether overtime was authorised; those checks sit with you as the approver.
Any time that is not approved by 10am Monday will be paid in the next pay run. It will not be estimated or entered manually, and the pay run will not be held while approvals are chased.
If you will be away on Monday morning, please either approve before you go or tell me now who is approving on your behalf.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E2  Friday, period closed

blocks.when: Friday, 4pm, the day the period closes
blocks.to: All approving managers, or only those with items outstanding
blocks.subject: Pay period now closed - timesheet approvals due 10am Monday [DD Mon]
body: Hi all,
The pay fortnight [DD Mon] to [DD Mon] has now closed. Approvals are due in Employment Hero by 10am Monday [DD Mon].
Still outstanding as at 4pm today:
[Manager name] - [n] timesheets
[Manager name] - [n] timesheets
[Manager name] - [n] timesheets
Also outstanding, no timesheet submitted at all:
[Employee name] - [cost centre] - please follow up with them directly
Any time not approved by 10am Monday will be paid in the next pay run. The pay run will not be held.
If anything here looks wrong, it is quicker to fix it today than on Monday morning.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E3  Monday, final call

blocks.when: Monday, 8am, two hours before the cut-off
blocks.cc: Their department heads, Graham, Duncan, accounts
blocks.subject: Final call: timesheet approvals close at 10am today - fortnight ending [DD Mon]
body: Hi [Name],
Approvals for the fortnight ending [DD Mon] close at 10am this morning. The following are still unapproved in Employment Hero:
[Employee name] - [n] shifts - [dates]
[Employee name] - [n] shifts - [dates]
After 10am these hours drop out of this fortnight's pay run and will be paid in the next one. I will not be able to add them in afterwards.
If there is a reason you cannot approve by 10am, tell me now and I will note it, but the cut-off does not move.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E4  Monday, cut-off passed

blocks.cc: Their department head, Graham, Duncan, accounts
blocks.subject: Cut-off passed: [n] timesheets unapproved, hours deferred to next pay run - fortnight ending [DD Mon]
body: Hi [Name],
The 10am cut-off for the fortnight ending [DD Mon] has now passed. The following timesheets were not approved and the hours have been excluded from this fortnight's pay run:
[Employee name] - [n] hours - [dates] - [cost centre]
[Employee name] - [n] hours - [dates] - [cost centre]
These hours will be paid in the pay run for the fortnight ending [DD Mon], as a back pay. Nothing is lost; the payment is one fortnight later.
Reminders were sent on [Thursday DD Mon], [Friday DD Mon] and at 8am this morning.
Please approve the timesheets when you can so the hours are picked up next fortnight. If the approval is still outstanding at the next cut-off the same thing will happen again.
[Department head name], flagging this for your visibility.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E5  Query back to an approver
For use when payroll spots something that looks wrong in an approved timesheet. It goes back to the approver with a deadline; it is not corrected in the pay run.

blocks.when: As soon as it is found, during reconciliation
blocks.subject: Query on an approved timesheet: [Employee name] - fortnight ending [DD Mon]
body: Hi [Name],
While processing the pay run I have come across the following on a timesheet you have approved:

[Employee name], [date]: [what the record shows] - [why it looks wrong, e.g. 14 hours recorded with no overtime approval attached / time in lieu recorded against a day with no rostered shift / no meal break recorded on a 9 hour shift]
I am not able to resolve this one; it is a question about what was worked and whether it was authorised, which sits with you as the approver.

Can you confirm either that the timesheet is correct as approved, or tell me what it should say, by [time] [today / tomorrow]. If I do not hear back before the pay run is finalised, I will process it exactly as approved, or exclude it and pay it next fortnight if it cannot be paid compliantly as it stands.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E6  Telling an employee their time moves to the next run
Send this only once the cut-off has passed and E4 has gone out. Keep it factual and do not editorialise about the manager.

blocks.subject: Part of your hours for [DD Mon] to [DD Mon] will be paid in the next pay run
body: Hi [Name],
I am letting you know that the following hours were not approved in Employment Hero before this fortnight's cut-off, so they are not in Tuesday's pay:
[date] - [n] hours
[date] - [n] hours
These hours will be paid in full in the next pay run, dated [DD Mon], as a back pay. Nothing has been lost and no further action is needed from you.
The rest of your pay for the fortnight is unaffected and will be paid on [DD Mon] as normal.
Approvals for the period are handled by [Manager name], who is copied here.
Thanks,
[Name]

blocks.text: E7  Announcing the change, once

The one-off email that puts the new arrangement in place. Send it over Duncan's or Graham's name rather than payroll's: a process change that reassigns accountability does not land coming from the person it benefits.

blocks.when: Once, at least one full fortnight before it takes effect
blocks.to: All approving managers and department heads
blocks.subject: Change to payroll timesheet approvals, effective fortnight ending [DD Mon]
body: All,
From the fortnight ending [DD Mon] we are formalising how timesheets are approved. The change is about who checks what; the deadlines and the systems are unchanged.
Approving managers are responsible for confirming, before approving a timesheet:
The hours recorded were actually worked
The actual times reconcile to the roster, or the difference is understood and accepted
Any overtime was authorised in advance, with the approval attached to the timesheet recording the reason, whether it is chargeable to the client, and whether it is paid or taken as time in lieu
Any time in lieu accrued or taken is correct against the roster
Meal breaks are recorded accurately
The cost centre on each shift is correct

Payroll is responsible for processing approved timesheets correctly: applying the award and the overtime matrix, verifying pay rates, balancing the pay run, and superannuation, PAYG and reporting. Payroll will not check hours against rosters and will not decide whether overtime or time in lieu was authorised. Those checks require knowledge of what was worked, which sits with the manager, not with payroll.
Two practical consequences:

Timesheets must be approved by 10am on the Monday of the processing week. Any time not approved by then will be paid in the next pay run. It will not be entered manually and the pay run will not be held.
Where payroll finds something that looks wrong on an approved timesheet, it will come back to the approving manager as a query rather than being corrected by payroll.
Please make sure a delegate is set up in Employment Hero for any period you are away, so approvals are not held up by leave.
[Duncan / Graham]

blocks.text: Using the templates

rows: The value is in being able to show the same notice went out every fortnight. Rewriting them each time undermines that
So the record sits with the role, not with whoever happened to be processing
Into the fortnight folder with the rest of the records, as described in Part 6. They are the evidence of notice
It is a one-off from Duncan or Graham. The fortnightly four come from payroll
Do not add the names of people who are up to date
E2, E3 and E4 go only to approvers with something outstanding. Copying everyone on an escalation that is not theirs is how people start ignoring the emails

blocks.text: The cycle at a glance
Payroll runs fortnightly. The pay period ends on a Friday, prep starts the same day, the run is processed on the Monday, and the money moves on the Tuesday.

rows: Payroll notes arrive in your inbox and the CTS Accounts inbox, collated into a single draft email as they come  (Part 1)
E1 advance notice to all approvers
The pay period closes. Prep starts the same day: the period runs Saturday to Friday, so the Friday it ends on is the Friday before the processing Monday
Timesheet template copied into the fortnight folder and populated, notes recorded  (Part 1)
E2 period closed, outstanding approvals named
Managers check hours against rosters, check overtime and time in lieu, and approve
E3 final call to anyone still outstanding
E4 escalation. Unapproved hours excluded and deferred to the next run
Gate: nothing under Submitted. Create the pay run  (Part 2)
Process the pay run employee by employee, applying the award and the matrix to approved hours  (Parts 3a, 3b, 3c)
Apply the payroll notes, accrue bonus leave if it is the last run of the month, verify rates, balance to zero  (Part 5)
Finalise, Graham approves, ABA file to CommBiz, funds transferred, Duncan notified, super created, five reports filed  (Part 6)
Pay date. Duncan approves the payment in CommBiz and it processes
Publish pay slips. Complete super and the ATO lodgement if either was deferred  (Part 6)

blocks.label: Four fixed points.
blocks.text: The recordings fix four things: prep starts the Friday before, the timesheet cut-off is 10am Monday, the pay date is always the Tuesday of the processing week, and pay slips are published the day after the payment is approved. Everything between the cut-off and the pay date runs on the Monday. The recordings never show that Monday's work split across two days, so treat Monday as a full day, not a morning.
The main line: seven stages

Each stage has a trigger that starts it and a gate that has to be satisfied before the next one begins. Skipping a gate does not save time; it means redoing the work after the problem surfaces further down.
Stage 1  Prep and the approval window

rows: The pay period closes on the Friday. Note collection has been running all fortnight

Collates the notes into one email for approval, copies the timesheet template into the fortnight folder, records every note, populates columns E to S only where the dollar value changes, and sends E1, E2 and E3 on schedule
Check hours against the roster, check that overtime and time in lieu are correct and authorised, and approve in Employment Hero by 10am Monday
10am Monday. Nothing under Submitted. Anything still unapproved is excluded and paid in the next run; E4 goes out at 10:05am
Part 1: Payroll Prep, and the emails above

blocks.label: Payroll no longer owns this gate's outcome.
blocks.text: Payroll owns sending the reminders on time and escalating at 10:05am. It does not own getting the approvals in, and it does not hold the pay run open waiting for them. That is the difference between the old process and this one.
Stage 2  Create the pay run

rows: The cut-off has passed and the approvals gate is resolved, one way or the other
Sets cell B1 to the fortnight period, re-checks Submitted is empty, creates the pay run on CTS - Fortnight with the pay date set to the Tuesday
Import Timesheets must be set to Timesheets for this pay period, never All unpaid timesheets
The payee count looks right for the fortnight. If it does not, delete the pay run and create it again rather than working through it
Part 2: Creating a New Pay Run

blocks.label: Nothing is committed yet.
blocks.text: Stage 2 is the last point where starting over is cheap. Deleting and recreating a wrongly built pay run takes minutes; correcting one employee by employee takes the afternoon.
Stage 3  Process the approved hours

This stage used to be reconciliation. Under the responsibility model it is not: the hours arrive certified by the approver, and payroll's job is to see that they are paid correctly under the award and the matrix, not to re-establish what was worked.

rows: The pay run exists and the payee count is right
Works the pay run in alphabetical order. Checks each person's employment type, then applies the correct award or matrix treatment to the hours as approved
Run the roster comparison, decide whether a long day was authorised, or decide whether hours should have been overtime or time in lieu. Those are queried back under E5
Employment Hero, the Live Performance Award, the CTS Overtime Matrix, the Excel timesheet
This is still the longest stage of the fortnight, and still where a non-compliant payment would originate
Every payee processed, hours transferred to the spreadsheet, verified rates marked green, queries sent on anything that cannot be paid as approved
Parts 3a, 3b and 3c. Which one applies is set out under Which path each employee takes, below

blocks.text: Stage 4  Apply the notes and adjustments

rows: Everyone in the pay run has been processed
Adds anyone still missing, then applies every payroll note: back pays, leave never captured, time in lieu adjustments, per diem at $75 a night
Back pays for hours that dropped out of the previous fortnight for want of an approval. These arrive here as a routine item, not an exception
If this is the last pay run of the month, accrues bonus leave from the tracker, a month ahead
Verifies every pay rate against the rate increase spreadsheet, and overrides any rate that failed to sync from HR
Nothing left to add. Anything applied after this point throws the balance out again

blocks.text: Stage 5  Balance

rows: Every adjustment is in and every rate is verified
Enters the Employment Hero totals against the per EH Payroll row and reads the two checksums
Hours checksum at zero means the processing is complete. Dollars out with hours agreeing means a rate or multiplier is wrong, usually an overtime rate on a stale base rate
Both checksums at zero, or the dollar figure within a couple of cents of rounding

blocks.label: Balance once, at the end.
blocks.text: Checking the totals early feels productive and is not. A single back pay applied afterwards puts the balance out again and the work is repeated. Get everything in first.
Stage 6  Finalise and pay

rows: Checks the pay period and paid date, finalises with Graham as approver, then waits
Logs in, reviews the total and approves. Nothing proceeds until he does
Refreshes, downloads the ABA file, imports it to CommBiz as Direct Entry with Set File as Modifiable ticked, submits and confirms
Cover net payroll plus super plus anything else scheduled, transferred from savings, leaving roughly a $20,000 buffer, described as MT payroll
Payroll email to Duncan, copying Graham, Danica and accounts, with the production summary and the transaction group screenshot. Then post in the payments chat tagging Duncan
Create Super Payment, then validate and confirm the batch separately

Five files into the fortnight folder: pay slips, pay run audit, ABA file, leave balances, leave liability. Both leave reports run to the period end date, not today. The four approval emails go in the same folder
Duncan approves the payment in CommBiz

blocks.label: This is the least reversible stage.
blocks.text: Once super payments have been made against a pay run, Employment Hero will not let you unlock it. Be confident the processing is complete before you finalise, not hopeful.
Stage 7  Next day close-out

rows: You have confirmed Duncan approved the payment
Publishes pay slips. This is what notifies employees, which is why it waits for the approval
Completes the super batch and the ATO lodgement if either was deferred
Sends E6 to anyone whose hours were deferred, if that has not already gone out
The fortnight is closed. The next one has already started collecting notes, and carries the deferred hours as back pay

blocks.text: The gates: six points where the process stops
These are the points where you cannot proceed until something is true. Three are payroll's to clear and three belong to somebody else.

rows: Payroll does not wait. The hours are excluded and paid next fortnight, and E4 goes out
The count at the top of the pay run looks right
Stop and investigate before working through the run
Reads zero before dollars are looked at
Keep working. Do not start on dollars
Zero, or within a couple of cents of rounding
Do not finalise. Read gross earnings employee by employee
The payment sits. No pay slips published. No documented backup

blocks.label: Gate 1 has changed; gates 5 and 6 have not.
blocks.text: Gate 1 used to be open-ended: payroll chased until the approvals came in. It now closes at 10am with a defined consequence. Gates 5 and 6 still depend on two named people with no documented backup, which remains the largest hole in this workflow.
Which path each employee takes

Stage 3 is not one procedure, it is three. Which applies depends on employment type and on whether the person's hours reach the pay run on their own. Check the type before applying any rule: the same hours are treated differently for a casual and a salaried employee.

rows: Live Performance Award: 1.75 above 38 hours in a week, overtime above 8 hours in a day, the meal-break rules, and no double-dipping between daily and weekly
That the hours are true and reconcile to the roster, and that any overtime was authorised
The hours, verified against the manager's own knowledge. PwC Australia and payment networks among others run no roster, so the approval is the only control
CTS Overtime Matrix, not the award. The 80-hour fortnight anchor and the 8-hour rounding rule
That the hours are true and that any overtime was pre-approved, with the basis recorded
Fixed hours from the rule on their login. Check the rate, which often comes through wrong
Nothing to approve; there are no timesheets. Confirm the arrangement is current
In the pay run but not the spreadsheet. Add at the rate excluding casual loading
The timesheet as for anyone else
Created in HR first, then synced. Watch the rounding rule pushing a short day back to eight hours
That the leave is approved and the dates are right
A missed shift from an earlier fortnight
The one case where you import unpaid timesheets instead of this pay period
The shift, retrospectively, before payroll will pay it

blocks.label: The manual-handling people are the ones that get missed.
blocks.text: Everyone in Parts 3a and 3b appears in the pay run, so working top to bottom finds them. The people in Part 3c can be absent altogether. Nothing prompts you; you have to know to look.
Branches off the main line
These sit outside the fortnightly sequence. Each has a settled answer, so the risk is not knowing the branch exists rather than not knowing what to do.
Hours that dropped out for want of an approval

The routine case now, rather than an exception. The hours were excluded at the cut-off, E4 and E6 have gone out, and the approval has since come through. Pay it in the current run as a back pay under Part 5, selecting only the affected dates. Nothing special is required and no separate authorisation is needed: the hours were worked and are now approved.
A timesheet approved with overtime or time in lieu that looks wrong

Query it back under E5 with a deadline. Do not correct it and do not pay it on your own reading. If the approver does not respond before the pay run is finalised, pay it exactly as approved where that is compliant, or exclude it and pay it next fortnight where it is not. Either way the record shows that payroll raised it and who did not answer.
A termination or final pay

Not part of the cycle. A resignation is paid through a small ad hoc pay run created for that person, usually because the final pay cannot wait for the next fortnight. The mechanics are the same as a normal run, but you strip the pay run back to the people you actually need, terminate inside it, and check the unused leave payout against the balances held in Employment Hero HR before finalising. Annual leave and time in lieu are paid out; personal and carer's leave and family and domestic violence leave are not. See Part 7.

blocks.label: A termination is the one case where deferring to the next run is not available.
blocks.text: There is no next pay run for someone who has left. Unapproved hours on a final pay have to be resolved before it is finalised, which means the approval has to be chased, and chased hard. Treat an outstanding approval on a termination as an immediate escalation to the department head, not a cut-off matter.
An expense submitted after the cut-off

It goes into the following pay run. Expenses only import if they were submitted before the cut-off, and there is no way to force a late one in. Entering it by hand risks the same expense importing again next fortnight and being paid twice. This has been the process since 2024, and it is the precedent the same rule for unapproved hours is built on.
An error found after finalising

Part 5 shows corrections being made as back pays in the following fortnight, which is the documented answer. Once super has been paid against the run it cannot be unlocked at all. What is not documented is whether an underpayment, or an error on a termination, has to be fixed immediately instead, and who decides. Ask before you need it.
A rate that did not sync from HR

A known Employment Hero fault leaves the old rate in payroll, often with a warning icon against the employee. This is payroll's, not the approver's: override the rate manually for the current run, then check whether earlier fortnights were paid at the stale rate and add a back pay if they were.
A casual needing access to a cost centre

Not part of any pay run. Most cost centres are available to everyone; casuals are the exception and have to be enabled individually under Payroll Settings, Locations. Do it on the payroll side, not in HR, where the setting only allows a single cost centre.

The left column is the symptom. The right is the first move. Where the recordings stop, it says so; those are the ones to get answers for before your first run rather than on the day.

A manager asks you to add unapproved hours
Decline and point at the rule: it is paid next fortnight. If they push, refer them to Graham. Do not make the exception yourself
Escalate immediately. There is no next pay run to defer to
The pay run will not balance
Hours first, then dollars. Read gross earnings employee by employee and check overtime rates before ordinary rates. No documented threshold for asking for help

Transfer from savings, covering net payroll plus super plus anything else scheduled, leaving a $20,000 buffer. How much notice the transfer needs to clear is not documented
Super and the ATO lodgement can slip to the next day; this happened during the Part 6 recording without consequence. What to do if the outage lands on the ABA upload is not documented

Not documented. The payment sits in CommBiz until approved
Back pay in the following fortnight. Whether an underpayment has to be fixed sooner is not documented

blocks.label: The one answer payroll must not give.
blocks.text: There is no version of this where payroll enters hours that nobody approved. Not as a favour, not because the employee is upset, not because the manager promises to approve it later. That single exception, made once, re-establishes that payroll will absorb the problem and the cut-off stops working from that fortnight on.
Known gaps
These are not oversights in the writing. They are things the training recordings never covered, or decisions this change raises that have not been made. Each needs an answer from Duncan or Graham.
Raised by this change

How far back a missed shift can be recovered before it needs handling differently, and who approves a back pay for a closed period
Whether there is a variance threshold below which a pay run can be finalised, or whether it must always be zero apart from rounding
The conversion for a contract rate quoted inclusive of casual loading, and whether the ex-loading rate can be looked up rather than calculated

blocks.label: Three of these matter more than the rest.
blocks.text: The two approver backups, the Employment Hero contact, and your escalation on pay day. Those are the ones you will need at the worst possible moment and cannot work out for yourself. Names, roles and phone numbers, written down somewhere you can find under pressure, before your first pay run rather than during it.

The responsibility model contradicts parts of the existing manual and checklist, which were written from the recordings and describe payroll doing the checks that now sit with approvers. Until those are updated the documents disagree with each other, and in a dispute the older ones will be quoted back at you. These are the specific places to fix.
